title: Beginner 1 · Everyday decisions to business basics
story: Start with three familiar situations, learn three business basics, then make two simple CNH connections. No financial-result memorization is required.

questions.prompt: The team is ready, but a required part has not arrived. What is limiting production right now?
options: Available people
The missing material
The shift length
The training schedule
questions.explanation: More people cannot make this product until its required material arrives. The missing part is the immediate constraint.
questions.discussion: Which constraint do we sometimes mistake for a staffing shortage?

valueConnection.why: Identify the immediate constraint before adding activity or complexity.

learning.definition: A constraint is the factor currently limiting useful output.
learning.lookFor: Read Constraint in the preparation guide, then search “Bottleneck” in Vocabulary for the related production idea. Picture dinner delayed by a missing ingredient. For a real plant decision, Operations should verify materials, equipment, and qualified people.
learning.prepare: Describe one reason a fully staffed team might still be unable to finish a job.

questions.prompt: A short backlog may need overtime. What should HR and Operations check before approving it?
options: Volunteer coverage and last month’s overtime
Base wages for the extra scheduled hours
Needed good output, qualified coverage, and total overtime cost
Budgeted headcount and remaining open jobs
questions.explanation: Overtime may help, but only if trained people, materials, and equipment can produce the needed good units. Include the overtime premium in the cost.
questions.discussion: What would make extra hours unproductive?

valueConnection.why: HR and Operations can agree on the output needed and the resources to deliver it.

learning.definition: Overtime adds working time and usually costs more per hour than regular time.
learning.lookFor: Read Overtime in the preparation guide. Ask whether extra hours would actually produce useful work or just add cost. For a real workplace decision, confirm qualified coverage, available materials, and the applicable overtime cost with Operations and Payroll.
learning.prepare: Imagine a team working two extra hours. Explain what needs to be ready for those hours to help.

questions.prompt: Only one person is qualified for a critical station. What would reduce the coverage risk?
options: Treat course attendance as job qualification
Count the whole shift as qualified coverage
Assign a backup before qualification
Train and qualify backup coverage
questions.explanation: Backup coverage needs the required skills and authorization. Headcount alone does not replace qualification.
questions.discussion: Which task needs a stronger backup plan?

valueConnection.why: Developing skills supports people’s growth while improving coverage.

learning.definition: Qualified coverage means people with the skills and authorization required for the work.
learning.lookFor: Read Qualified Coverage in the preparation guide, then search “Skill matrix” in Vocabulary. A full team does not mean everyone can do a specialist task. For actual work, Operations should verify training, qualifications, and coverage.
learning.prepare: Choose a task at home or work that needs a specific skill. Explain what a backup would need to learn before taking over.

options: The amount earned from selling products or services
Money borrowed from a bank
The wages paid to employees
The cost of parts purchased
questions.explanation: Revenue is what the business earns from selling products or services. A loan brings cash in, but it is not sales revenue.
questions.discussion: Why does cash coming in not always mean revenue?

valueConnection.why: A clear definition makes financial conversations easier to follow.

learning.definition: Revenue is the amount earned from sales before subtracting business costs.
learning.lookFor: Read Revenue in the preparation guide. For a public company example, open Quarter decoder and find “Net sales” for Industrial Activities or “Revenue” for Financial Services. Check the selected period and business scope; the number does not tell you profit.
learning.prepare: Explain why money from a customer sale is revenue but money from a bank loan is not.

questions.prompt: In a simplified practice example, sales are $100 and all costs are $80. What is profit?
questions.explanation: Sales minus all costs gives profit: $100 minus $80 equals $20. Real reports distinguish several profit measures, so read the label.
questions.discussion: Can sales rise while profit falls? What would have to happen to costs?

valueConnection.why: Start with the basic relationship before introducing more detailed measures.

learning.definition: Profit is what remains after the relevant costs are subtracted from revenue.
learning.lookFor: Read Profit in the preparation guide and try sales minus costs. To explore a real result, search “Adjusted EBIT” in Vocabulary and read its definition. Real profit measures include different costs, so Finance must validate the measure for an actual business decision.
learning.prepare: Try sales of $150 and all costs of $100. Explain what remains and why sales alone do not show profit.

questions.prompt: Parts have been purchased but are still waiting to be used. What does that mean for cash?
options: The purchase used no cash until the parts are consumed
Some cash is tied up in inventory
The parts create profit as soon as they are purchased
The purchase counts as customer revenue
questions.explanation: Money spent on parts is no longer available as cash. Those parts are inventory until they are used or sold; collecting from customers is a separate step.
questions.discussion: Which inventory can we reduce without disrupting customer delivery?

valueConnection.why: Understanding inventory helps improve flow and use resources well.

learning.definition: Inventory includes materials and products held for future use or sale. It can tie up cash.
learning.lookFor: Read Inventory in the preparation guide, then search “Working capital” in Vocabulary. Think of groceries already paid for but still in the cupboard: useful stock is different from spendable cash. For real company figures, ask the controller how inventory and payment timing are measured.
learning.prepare: Explain why a warehouse full of purchased parts is different from a bank account full of cash.

questions.prompt: A farming customer has less money available after paying operating costs. How might that affect a new machine purchase?
options: They may delay it or look for financing
Their replacement budget is unaffected by available cash
Borrowing makes their cash position irrelevant
Crop prices alone determine their ability to buy
questions.explanation: A customer with less available money may delay replacement or need financing. This is a possible response, not a prediction for every customer.
questions.discussion: What would you want to know before treating a demand forecast as a staffing plan?

valueConnection.why: Connecting decisions to customers’ needs and finances keeps their perspective central.

learning.definition: Customer demand depends partly on whether customers need a product and can afford to buy it.
learning.lookFor: Open Business drivers and read “Farmer cash is the link to equipment” and the “Farmer economics” tab. The linked USDA farm-income page is public background; you do not need to memorize figures. For a real staffing plan, validate customer demand with the business.
learning.prepare: Imagine you need a new car but have less cash after paying bills. Explain how that could affect when or how you buy it.

questions.prompt: You want to understand a CNH financial result you do not recognize. What is the best first step?
options: Compare headline results without checking business scope
Use revenue as the profit measure
Use a full-year total for any quarterly comparison
Check the measure, business scope, period, and source notes
questions.explanation: First identify what the number measures, which business it covers, and the period. Quarter decoder and the linked source notes are places to start.
questions.discussion: Which part of a financial report would you ask someone to clarify?

valueConnection.why: A few clear questions make a detailed result easier to understand.

learning.definition: A financial figure needs a measure, a business scope, a period, and an evidence source to be interpreted.
learning.lookFor: Open Quarter decoder, choose a reporting period and business scope, then read a measure and its note. Open the public CNH results link to check the original report and definitions. You can do this without a CNH login; start by understanding one number rather than memorizing it.
learning.prepare: Find one measure in Quarter decoder. Say what it measures, which business it covers, and whether it describes a quarter or six months.

title: Beginner 2 · Practice the basics again
story: Start with three familiar situations, learn three business basics, then make two simple CNH connections. No financial-result memorization is required.

questions.prompt: Orders are expected to slow. What should the team check before changing staffing schedules?
options: Open requisitions and the hiring budget
Confirmed production needs, critical skills, and available coverage
Last year’s staffing at the same time
The regional sales headline alone
questions.explanation: Start with the actual production plan and the skills required to deliver it. A broad market headline alone does not tell you the plant’s staffing need.
questions.discussion: What information is missing when someone says we need fewer people?

valueConnection.why: Shared planning connects people decisions with operating needs.

learning.definition: A production plan connects demand, output timing, and the resources required to deliver.
learning.lookFor: Read Production Plan in the preparation guide. For the CNH connection, open Business drivers and select “Production & skills.” A headline about fewer orders is a starting signal; an actual schedule needs confirmed work, timing, and qualified coverage verified with Operations.
learning.prepare: Imagine preparing meals for a party. What would you need to know about guest numbers, timing, and available help before changing the plan?

questions.prompt: Some units need to be repaired before shipment. Why does this matter to the business?
options: Completed assembly means the units count as good shipments
Repair hours reduce cost per good unit
Rework uses time and resources before good units can ship
Higher assembly speed offsets all rework losses
questions.explanation: Rework consumes labor, material, or equipment time. Counting completed work without checking quality can overstate what is ready to ship.
questions.discussion: Where should we measure good output rather than activity alone?

valueConnection.why: Reliable quality helps deliver products customers can use.

learning.definition: Rework is additional work needed to bring a product to the required standard.
learning.lookFor: Read Rework in the preparation guide, then search “First-pass yield” in Vocabulary. Think of a job that must be fixed before it can be used. For actual production, Quality and Operations should distinguish finished good units from units awaiting repair.
learning.prepare: Explain why counting every item worked on can overstate how many are ready for a customer.

questions.prompt: A trained operator is absent from a critical station. What should the supervisor check first?
options: Whether qualified backup coverage is available
Whether any available person can be assigned immediately
Whether the shift’s total headcount meets plan
Whether yesterday’s output met the target
questions.explanation: Check for a qualified backup and follow the required operating and safety procedures. An available person may not have the right qualification.
questions.discussion: How could cross-training improve tomorrow’s coverage?

valueConnection.why: Matching work to qualified coverage respects people and the skills they need.

learning.definition: Shift coverage is the availability of the right qualified people for the work scheduled.
learning.lookFor: Read Shift Coverage in the preparation guide, then search “Skill matrix” in Vocabulary. The useful question is who can cover the required task, not just how many people are present. For an actual shift, the responsible supervisor should verify qualified backup coverage.
learning.prepare: Imagine the only trained person for a task is absent. Explain why another available person may need training before filling in.

questions.prompt: A customer receives a product today but will pay later. Which statement is most useful?
options: Delivery means the cash is already available
Recorded profit is available cash to spend
Revenue is recorded only when cash reaches the bank
The sale and cash collection may happen at different times
questions.explanation: A sale can be recorded before the customer pays. Profit and cash therefore need separate attention; ask Finance about the actual accounting and payment terms.
questions.discussion: What happens to available cash while we wait for a customer to pay?

valueConnection.why: Separating profit from cash avoids a common misunderstanding.

learning.definition: Cash timing describes when money is actually received or paid, which can differ from when sales or costs are recorded.
learning.lookFor: Read Cash Timing in the preparation guide, then search “Working capital” in Vocabulary. Picture delivering a product today and receiving payment next month: the sale and money received have different dates. For an actual business, Finance should confirm payment terms and accounting treatment.
learning.prepare: Explain why a business may need cash to pay bills while it waits for customers to pay.

questions.prompt: In a simplified example, total production cost is $2,000 for 100 good units. What is cost per good unit?
questions.explanation: Divide the total cost by good units: $2,000 divided by 100 equals $20 per good unit. The example is fictional and excludes any separate costs not stated.
questions.discussion: How would more scrap affect cost per good unit if total cost stayed the same?

valueConnection.why: Measuring useful output helps judge performance and improvement.

learning.definition: Cost per good unit divides a defined cost by output that meets the required standard.
learning.lookFor: Read Cost Per Good Unit in the preparation guide. Divide the stated total cost by units that meet the required standard, using the practice numbers in the question. For a real comparison, the controller and Operations should agree which costs and good units are counted.
learning.prepare: Try $600 of total cost for 30 good units. Explain what happens to cost per good unit if fewer units are good and the total cost stays the same.

questions.prompt: One step can handle 80 units per shift, while every other required step can handle 100. What limits this simple process?
options: The average capacity of all steps
The fastest step
The step that can handle 80 units
The total number of people alone
questions.explanation: In this simplified process, the 80-unit step is the bottleneck. Improving a different step alone will not raise the process’s maximum output.
questions.discussion: Which assumption should we verify before using a simple capacity model?

valueConnection.why: Focus on the limiting step before spreading effort across the whole process.

learning.definition: A bottleneck is the process step whose available capacity currently limits the flow.
learning.lookFor: Read Bottleneck in the preparation guide, or search the same word in Vocabulary. In Business drivers, scroll to “Can the plan actually run?” and try fictional capacity inputs. For a real production plan, Operations should verify the process and each capacity assumption.
learning.prepare: Imagine three steps that can each handle 80, 100, and 100 units. Explain which step limits the process and where an improvement would help.

questions.prompt: In a practice scenario, a CNH customer needs a machine during harvest. Why could faster, reliable repair support matter?
options: It can help the customer return the machine to work
Faster repairs eliminate the customer’s downtime cost
More repair activity means the customer is more productive
Shorter repair time proves the fault is fixed
questions.explanation: Reliable repair support can reduce time the machine is unavailable. The connection is the customer’s ability to do the work, not a guaranteed financial outcome.
questions.discussion: Which workforce capability supports reliable customer service?

valueConnection.why: Reliable support starts with the work the customer needs to complete.

learning.definition: Uptime is the time equipment is available to do its intended work.
learning.lookFor: Read Customer Uptime in the preparation guide. Picture needing a working car to get to an appointment: reliable repair helps it return to use. For the CNH connection, open the public company page and read “Built around customers.” Actual service plans need the business team to verify customer needs and service skills.
learning.prepare: Explain how reliable repair or backup support can help someone complete the work they need to do.

questions.prompt: You are unsure whether a staffing proposal really saves money. What should you do next?
options: Count training attendance as proof of savings
Use the lowest wage rate as the entire cost
Assume any headcount reduction guarantees savings
Ask the controller to validate total cost, good output, and cash timing
questions.explanation: HR can frame the people options, Operations can test delivery and skills, and Finance can validate the financial assumptions. Asking a precise question is part of learning.
questions.discussion: What evidence would persuade you that the claimed benefit is real?

valueConnection.why: Different teams can combine their expertise to test a proposal fairly.

learning.definition: A business case connects an action to expected benefits, costs, timing, and evidence.
learning.lookFor: Read Asking Finance in the preparation guide. Use Vocabulary to look up unfamiliar terms, such as “Product Cost” or “Working capital.” For a real proposal, bring its costs, useful output, and timing assumptions to Finance and Operations for validation; you do not need internal records for this practice round.
learning.prepare: Imagine someone says a change will save money. Ask: what changes, which costs and benefits count, and when does money actually move?
